A survey on marriage in Japan found that 25% of couples who wed within a year of their first meeting used a dating app.

* English
* 日本語
* 简体字
* 繁體字
* Français
* Español
* العربية
* Русский

An online survey on marriage in Japan conducted in October by Meiji Yasuda Life Insurance found that 31.2% of respondents said they first met their spouses as coworkers in the workplace. The next most common way to meet was through being introduced by a friend, at 23.6%, followed by those who were former classmates, at 12.5%. Among couples who got married within a year of first meeting, 25% used a dating app, while another 25% met at work.

The survey targeted married people aged 20 to 79 across Japan. There were 1,620 responses from 810 men and 810 women.

[![How did you meet your spouse? (All survey respondents)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2507278/2507278.png)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2507278/2507278.png)

[![How did you meet your spouse? (Respondents who got married within a year)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2507279/2507279.png)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2507279/2507279.png)

When asked about their motivation for using dating apps, comments from respondents included: “It’s an easy way to meet people”; “Because it’s hard to meet people at work”; “It makes it possible to choose a type of person I like.”

Amid the pandemic, fewer married couples met through the workplace as companies limited outside events and shifted to remote work, but in the current survey the percentage of such couples rose by 10 percentage points compared to the previous survey.

Overall, 15.4% of the respondents have actively engaged in spouse-hunting activities known as *konkatsu*. Such activities were most common among those in their thirties, with nearly one in five, or 21.1%, taking part before getting married.

[![Participation in Spouse-Hunting Activities by Age Group](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2507280/2507280.png)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2507280/2507280.png)

The most common spouse-hunting method by age group, according to the survey, was dating apps among respondents in their twenties (51%), matchmaking parties and events among those in their thirties (50.9%), and group dates or *gōkon* among those in their forties (48.9%), reflecting the different trends among different generations.

Aug 24, 2023

The last week of July and the first week of August alone each saw more than 10,000 people needing emergency transportation to the hospital for heatstroke in Japan.

* English
* 日本語
* 简体字
* 繁體字
* Français
* Español
* العربية
* Русский

Japan is still enduring the sweltering heat of summer; Fire and Disaster Management Agency statistics show that the number of people needing emergency transportation to the hospital because of heatstroke has been at a high level since July. More than 10,000 people were rushed to hospital in both the last week of July and the first week of August.

[![Weekly Emergency Transportation Cases for Heatstroke in Japan](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2452274/2452274.png)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2452274/2452274.png)

[![Locations Where Heatstroke Occurred (August 7–13)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2452194/2452194.png)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2452194/2452194.png)

[![Age Range for Heatstroke Cases (August 7–13)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2452195/2452195.png)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2452195/2452195.png)

There was an average of 1,295 annual deaths from heatstroke over the last five years until 2022. More than 80% of those cases involved seniors aged over 65, who tend to be less able to regulate their body temperature. The most common place for deaths caused by heatstroke, surprisingly, was indoors, such as residences, and around 90% of those who died had either not been using or did not own an air-conditioner. It is important in hot weather to use air-conditioning properly as well as to make sure to keep replenishing one’s intake of water and salt before starting to feel thirsty.

The Ministry of the Environment and Japan Meteorological Agency issue [heatstroke alerts](https://www.wbgt.env.go.jp/en/) to prompt people to take preventative action when the weather conditions make the risk of heatstroke extremely high. If an alert is issued, one should take more precautions than usual to prevent heatstroke, including using air-conditioning both day and night, avoiding going out unless necessary, and canceling or postponing any sports activities. It is also important to pay close attention to any elderly people, children, and people with disabilities around one.

The Japan Tourism Agency provides a safety information app. As well as information about earthquakes and tsunami, it can send out notifications when a heatstroke alert is issued.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/30/Tokyo_detention_center.jpg/250px-Tokyo_detention_center.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tokyo_detention_center.jpg)

[Tokyo Detention House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo_Detention_House "Tokyo Detention House"), which houses one of Japan's seven [execution chambers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Execution_chamber "Execution chamber")

[Capital punishment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_punishment "Capital punishment") is a legal penalty in [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan"). The [Penal Code of Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penal_Code_of_Japan "Penal Code of Japan") and several laws list 14 capital crimes, though in practice it is applied only for [aggravated murder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder_in_Japanese_law#Aggravated_murder "Murder in Japanese law"). Executions are carried out by [long drop hanging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanging#Long_drop "Hanging"), and take place at one of the seven execution chambers located in major cities across the country. The only crime punishable by a mandatory death sentence is instigation of foreign aggression.

Death sentences are usually passed in cases of multiple murders, although there have been some extremely grave cases where individuals who committed a single murder have been sentenced to death and executed, such as those involving torture, extreme brutality or kidnapping with a demand for ransom.[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-precedents-2)

Between January 2000 and July 2022, 98 inmates have been executed in Japan.[[3]](#cite_note-3) As of 28 June 2025, 105 [death row](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_row "Death row") inmates were awaiting execution.[[4]](#cite_note-nyt-shiraishi-4) The most recent execution was that of [Takahiro Shiraishi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takahiro_Shiraishi "Takahiro Shiraishi") on 27 June 2025.[[5]](#cite_note-5) Japan is one of four [developed democracies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Developed_countries "Developed countries") worldwide to actively apply the death penalty.[[a]](#cite_note-6)[[6]](#cite_note-7) In 2025, a government survey showed that about 83.1% of the Japanese population supports the death penalty.[[7]](#cite_note-8) The figure was a 2.3% increase from a survey taken five years prior.

According to the *[Kojiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kojiki "Kojiki")*, Japan's oldest historical book, the death penalty is believed to have first appeared in Japan in the first half of the 5th century during the reign of [Emperor Nintoku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_Nintoku "Emperor Nintoku"). Methods of execution during this period included strangulation, [beheading](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beheading#Japan "Beheading"), and burning to death, and in some special cases, the death penalty was carried out and then exposed to public view.[[8]](#cite_note-horj-9)

The [Taihō Code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taih%C5%8D_Code "Taihō Code") and the [Yōrō Code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Y%C5%8Dr%C5%8D_Code "Yōrō Code") stipulated two methods of capital punishment: beheading and strangulation. In 773, the method of beating to death was added for arsonists and thieves, bringing the total to three methods of capital punishment. The execution of the death penalty required the approval of the emperor.[[8]](#cite_note-horj-9)

Beginning in the [Nara period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nara_period "Nara period") (710–794), the death penalty was infrequently used, and the death penalty was abolished completely in the [Heian period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heian_period "Heian period") (794–1185). The death penalty was not used for 346 years following the execution of [Fujiwara no Nakanari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fujiwara_no_Nakanari "Fujiwara no Nakanari") in 810, until it was revived during the [Hōgen rebellion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C5%8Dgen_rebellion "Hōgen rebellion") of 1156. However, during the [Genpei War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genpei_War "Genpei War") (1180–1185), the death penalty by sawing and crucifixion may have been carried out.[[9]](#cite_note-10)[[8]](#cite_note-horj-9)

During the [Kamakura period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamakura_period "Kamakura period") (1185–1333), the only method of capital punishment was beheading, and felons in particular were displayed to the public as an example after their execution. The [Muromachi period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muromachi_period "Muromachi period") (1333–1573) largely followed the Kamakura period method of capital punishment. On the other hand, [seppuku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seppuku "Seppuku"), which appeared as a method of suicide in the Heian period, was first used as a method of capital punishment in this period.[[8]](#cite_note-horj-9)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article is about smart card for ID. For national identification number, see [Individual Number](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Individual_Number "Individual Number"). Not to be confused with the mandatory residency card required for foreign residents of Japan, the [Zairyū card](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zairyū_card "Zairyū card").

The **My Number Card** ([Japanese](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_language "Japanese language"): マイナンバーカード, [Hepburn](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hepburn_romanization "Hepburn romanization"): *mai nanbā kādo*), officially **Individual Number Card** ([Japanese](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_language "Japanese language"): 個人番号カード, [Hepburn](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hepburn_romanization "Hepburn romanization"): *kojin bangō kādo*), is an [identity document](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Identity_document "Identity document") issued to citizens of [Japan](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan") and foreign residents which contains a unique 12-digit [Individual Number](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Individual_Number "Individual Number") ([Japanese](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_language "Japanese language"): 個人番号, [Hepburn](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hepburn_romanization "Hepburn romanization"): *kojin bangō*) that serves as a [national identification number](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_identification_number "National identification number") in Japan.[[1]](#cite_note-1) Unlike similar-looking [identity cards in Europe](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_identity_cards_in_the_European_Economic_Area_and_Switzerland "National identity cards in the European Economic Area and Switzerland"), the My Number Card can be issued to both Japanese citizens and foreign residents, and is not proof of nationality. The My Number Card is used in Japan to streamline administrative purposes like filing taxes and social security, and it is also utilized to provide disaster response to those in need. It is the [de facto](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_facto "De facto") Japanese equivalent to a U.S. [Social Security Number](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Security_number "Social Security number").[[2]](#cite_note-2)

The My Number Card stores information such as personal name, photo, address, birthday, and sex. Residents who wish to obtain the card can request an application form from the municipality (via a ward office or city hall) where they reside.

Many countries around the world, including Japan, require residents and citizens to [disclose and register their address with the government](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resident_registration "Resident registration") for various bureaucratic purposes. Many countries obligate that their residents and citizens provide up to date information regarding [where they reside](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domicile_(law) "Domicile (law)"), by visiting a [registration office](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Registration_office "Registration office") or the [police](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police "Police") within a few days after establishing a new residence. However some countries, like the United States or Canada, do not require their residents or citizens to provide this information to the government, unless they are applying for a passport or drivers license.

Both Japanese citizens and foreign residents are obligated to report their [domicile](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domicile_(law) "Domicile (law)") to their nearest municipal government office.

During Japan’s Edo period, a number of domains in the west of the country were economically powerful, despite being far from the capital of Edo.

Japan’s [five richest domains](https://www.nippon.com/en/japan-data/h01683/) in the Edo period (1603–1868) included Kaga in what is now [Ishikawa](https://www.nippon.com/en/guide-to-japan/pref17/) Prefecture and Satsuma ([Kagoshima](https://www.nippon.com/en/guide-to-japan/pref46/) Prefecture), which was the wealthiest in western Japan.

The next richest five domains, rounding out the top 10, were all in the west of the country and ruled by *tozama* daimyō, those leaders who only submitted to [Tokugawa Ieyasu](https://www.nippon.com/en/japan-topics/b06907/) after he secured control of the country in the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600, or shortly before. Although such daimyō were considered low-ranking outsiders, based far from Edo (now Tokyo), there were several wealthy domains.

The *koku* was a measurement used in estimating a domains’ economic scale and was equivalent to around 180 liters of rice, or ¥300,000 in today’s terms according to calculations in *Edo no kakeibo* [Edo Account Books], edited by Isoda Michifumi. It was also a rough measure for the amount of rice one adult would eat each year.

## 6. Hosokawa clan, Kumamoto domain: 540,000 *koku* (¥162.0 billion), *tozama*

Hosokawa Tadaoki fought alongside Tokugawa Ieyasu at the Battle of Sekigahara and was awarded the small Kokura domain (now [Fukuoka](https://www.nippon.com/en/guide-to-japan/pref40/) Prefecture) in Kyūshū. His son Tadatoshi married Ieyasu’s Chiyohime, strengthening ties with the ruling family.

In 1632, punishment of another Kyūshū daimyō in the Katō clan and reallocation of his land to Tadatoshi brought an increase to 540,000 *koku*—this larger domain was roughly equivalent to today’s [Kumamoto](https://www.nippon.com/en/guide-to-japan/pref43/) Prefecture. Appointment of agricultural administrators boosted output, particularly sweet potatoes grown in the fertile volcanic soil of [Mount Aso](https://www.nippon.com/en/japan-data/h00439/).

Although the domain no longer exists, the current head of the clan is Hosokawa Morihiro, who was prime minister of Japan from 1993 to 1994.

## 7. Kuroda clan, Fukuoka domain: 473,000 *koku* (¥141.9 billion), *tozama*

Kuroda Nagamasa established the Fukuoka domain (now Fukuoka Prefecture) after territory was awarded to him for helping to bring over the daimyō Kobayakawa Hideaki to Ieyasu’s side at the Battle of Sekigahara. The leader Kuroda Tsugutaka is remembered for measures to alleviate poverty and rebuild domain finances after the Kyōhō Famine from 1732, as well as his support for [nō theater](https://www.nippon.com/en/views/b02332/).

[![A map of Fukuoka in the early nineteenth century shows the castle town close to the sea, suggesting burgeoning trade. (Courtesy Kyūshū University Library)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2427560/2427560.jpg)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2427560/2427560.jpg)  
A map of Fukuoka in the early nineteenth century shows the castle town close to the sea, suggesting burgeoning trade. (Courtesy Kyūshū University Library)

## 8. Asano clan, Hiroshima domain: 426,000 *koku* (¥127.8 billion), *tozama*

The Hiroshima domain (now [Hiroshima](https://www.nippon.com/en/guide-to-japan/pref34/) Prefecture) was ruled from 1619 by the Asano clan after the daimyō Fukushima Masanori was demoted for such offenses as making unauthorized repairs to his castle. Asano Nagaakira built up the economy through employing skilled administrators and making profits in the rice markets.

[![Father and son Asano Nagamasa and Nagaakira are enshrined at Nigitsu Shrine in Hiroshima. (© Pixta)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2427556/2427556.jpg)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2427556/2427556.jpg)  
Father and son Asano Nagamasa and Nagaakira are enshrined at Nigitsu Shrine in Hiroshima. (&© Pixta)

## 9. Mōri clan, Chōshū domain: 369,000 *koku* (¥110.7 billion), *tozama*

The Chōshū domain was ruled by the Mōri clan, which had dominated the Chūgoku region in western Japan under Mōri Motonari in the sixteenth century. As Motonari’s grandson nominally lined up on the opposite side to Ieyasu at the Battle of Sekigahara, his territory was reduced to the Chōshū domain (now [Yamaguchi](https://www.nippon.com/en/guide-to-japan/pref35/) Prefecture).

The domain worked hard to reduce the expense of traveling to Edo under the [*sankin kōtai* system](https://www.nippon.com/en/japan-topics/c08601/), and to settle its debts. In the eighteenth century, it became richer through the development of new rice fields, construction of ports, and making loans to shipping companies operating on the Seto Inland Sea. The domain was known for its production of rice, salt, paper, and wax.

It became a major opponent of the shogunate in the years leading up to the [Meiji Restoration](https://www.nippon.com/en/views/b06902/).

A survey in Japan found that two in three people sometimes sit in a train’s priority seats.

* English
* 日本語
* 简体字
* 繁體字
* Français
* Español
* العربية
* Русский

A recent online survey in Japan conducted by Wakamoto Pharmaceutical revealed that, at 66.9%, two in three of the 1,949 respondents sometimes sit in a priority seat on a train.

[![Do you ever sit in a priority seat on the train?](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2493726/2493726.png)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2493726/2493726.png)

The most common reason for sitting in a priority seat, given by 618 respondents, was “I planned to give up the seat if someone needed it.” A further 501 people said that “I was in the way if I stood up and the seat was available.” It seemed that many people held the perception that they were not planning to sit in the priority seat all the time, and only used it because it was available at that time.

[![Reason for Sitting in a Priority Seat](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2493730/2493730.png)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2493730/2493730.png)

Among those who did not sit in the priority seats, 65% believed “they need to be left available for those who need them.”

[![Reason for Not Sitting in a Priority Seat](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2493737/2493737.png)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2493737/2493737.png)

Regarding the [maternity mark](https://www.nippon.com/en/nipponblog/m00051/) indicating that someone is pregnant, there was extremely high awareness, with 85% of all respondents saying they knew it.

[![Do you know about the maternity mark?](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2493732/2493732.png)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2493732/2493732.png)

Nearly 80% said “I would give up my seat (even if I was sitting in a regular seat)” if they saw someone with a maternity mark badge and when combined with those who said “I would give up my seat if I was sitting in a priority seat,” this rose to 94%.

[![Would you give up your seat to someone with a maternity mark badge?](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2493733/2493733.png)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2493733/2493733.png)

The survey revealed that 54.9% had given up their seat for someone who was pregnant. Along with “I will always give up my seat for someone who needs it,” other reasons for people giving up their seat were based on easily understandable visual cues, including “they had a maternity mark badge,” “they had a large tummy,” and “it looked like they were struggling standing.”

While Japan’s food self-sufficiency on a calorie basis remained unchanged at 38% in fiscal 2022, on a production value basis it fell by five percentage points to 58%, due to high prices for grain, feed, and fertilizer, in addition to the weak yen.

* English
* 日本語
* 简体字
* 繁體字
* Français
* Español
* العربية
* Русский

Japan’s food self-sufficiency ratio for fiscal 2022 based on production value fell to a record low of 58% according to data compiled by the Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry, and Fisheries, for a year-on-year decrease of five percentage points. Even though food imports were at the same level as the previous year, the value of imports swelled due to soaring international prices for grain, feed, and fertilizer combined with the falling Japanese yen. The self-sufficiency rate is 17 points lower than the target for fiscal 2030 set by the government of 75% self-sufficiency in terms of production value.

Meanwhile, Japan’s food self-sufficiency on a calorie basis was 38%, unchanged from the previous year. Negative factors were the return to normal harvests for wheat and soybeans, after the bumper crops in fiscal 2021, as well as declines in the haul of mackerel and other fish. These factors were balanced by the fall in the consumption of oil and fats, which are dependent on imports. The fall in self-sufficiency levelled off in fiscal 2020 around 37%, but Japan is far from reaching the government target of 45% for calorie-based food self-sufficiency by fiscal 2030.

The food self-sufficiency rate is calculated by excluding livestock products produced using imported feed in order to gain an accurate understanding of domestic production. However, the domestic production rate does not reflect the feed self-sufficiency rate based on the view that all livestock products raised within Japan are domestically produced. The difference between the self-sufficiency rate and the domestic production rate indicates the degree of dependence on foreign feed.

[![Japan’s Food Self-Sufficiency and Domestic Production Rates](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2449695/2449695.png)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2449695/2449695.png)

[![Supply of Japan’s Calories by Country](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2449688/2449688.png)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2449688/2449688.png)

[![Production Value of Food Consumed in Japan by Country](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2449696/2449696.png)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2449696/2449696.png)

The calorie-based food self-sufficiency rates of major grain exporters Canada, Australia, and the United States, are well above 100%. Italy, which exports many high-priced vegetables and fruits, also has a strong self-sufficiency rate in terms of production value. Japan’s self-sufficiency rate for both calories and production value remains low compared to other countries.

[![Food Self-Sufficiency Rate by Country](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2449697/2449697.png)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2449697/2449697.png)

While it was once common for Japanese companies to have a negative view of employees who left before retirement, recent labor shortages are encouraging them to reconsider these corporate alumni.

* English
* 日本語
* 简体字
* 繁體字
* Français
* Español
* العربية
* Русский

In recent years, Japanese companies are showing more interest in “alumni recruitment,” or the rehiring of former employees who have either left or retired.

A survey on HR management conducted by Recruit Holdings, with responses from 2,761 HR managers at companies with 30 or more employees, found that the most common recruitment method (51.1% of those surveyed) is to rely on the government’s employment service Hello Work. This was followed by recruitment via the company’s website (46.3%). Recruitment through a company’s “alumni network,” meanwhile, remains a less common method, at 12.3%.

[![Methods Currently Used to Recruit Employees](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2473821/2473821.png)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2473821/2473821.png)

At the same time, however, 55.5% of those surveyed said that they are willing to rehire former employees who had either left the company or retired. The results of the Recruit survey suggest that even if corporate alumni networks are not recognized clearly as a recruitment tool, they are in fact being used by a majority of companies. From this one can conclude that such networks are likely to become an effective channel for employee recruitment in the future.

[![Is your company willing to rehire former employees?](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2473822/2473822.png)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2473822/2473822.png)

When asked about the state of their utilization of human resources over the past couple years, concerning the number of personnel and their level of ability (in terms of meeting job requirements), 42.9% of the companies that make use of corporate alumni recruitment were either “fully” or “somewhat” able to secure the needed number of employees, as opposed to 31.6% among companies that do not make use of former employees.

Further, 34.5% of companies that have implemented alumni recruitment said their level of human resources was either “fully” or “somewhat” adequate, as opposed to 24.6% among companies that did not make use of such recruitment. This survey result seems to indicate it is more effective to secure human resources by means of an alumni network. Some of the positive factors cited by the respondents include a better match between employees and the job due to an understanding of a company’s business style and corporate culture, a wider range of job-related abilities through obtaining new skills and perspectives from different environments, and the sense that returning employees can get up and running right away because they understand work procedures and internal relations.

Over half of international students looking to work in Japan after graduation received offers from firms compared to 86% of Japanese students.

* English
* 日本語
* 简体字
* 繁體字
* Français
* Español
* العربية
* Русский

International students in Japan are enjoying greater job prospects amid a labor crunch as the economy continues to rebound from the downturn caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. A survey of 362 international students registered with job-hunting site Career-Tasu run by Disco Inc. found that 52.5% had received job offers (including informal offers) as of July 2023, up from 48.0% the previous year. This is the highest figure for international students since 2017, when the current job-hunting schedule for students at Japanese universities was introduced. The figure reflects the improved job market in Japan, although the level of job offers for international students is still far lower than for Japanese students at 86.0%.

A total of 62.1% of international students engaged in job-hunting activities, including those who had received promises of employment from companies. This is more than double the 25.7% of Japanese students who were job hunting during the same period.

Japanese university students typically start job hunting around April to June of their third year, whereas international students tend to start in April of their fourth year, a difference that may impact the results of the latter group. An international student from Taiwan who was part of the survey explained that “until I complete my dissertation, I can’t start looking for a job with peace of mind,” while a Vietnamese student lamented that “many companies close their recruitment early, so I wasn’t able to prepare in time.”

[![Job Hunting Status as of July 2023](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2467647/2467647.png)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2467647/2467647.png)

The survey also asked what key points students wanted companies to consider when hiring. Leading the list was “communication skills,” which was mentioned by 58.3% of international students and a little less than 50% of Japanese students. Other leading answers among international students included “language skills,” “basic academic skills,” and “cross-cultural competence,” reflecting the hope among many students that companies will value the skills honed through studying abroad.

[![Key Points International Students Want Companies to Consider](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2467668/2467668.png)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2467668/2467668.png)

Eel is a traditional summer food in Japan, but overfishing led to the Japanese eel being designated as endangered.

The average market price for eel in Japan in May 2023 was ¥5,553 per kilogram, according to statistics based on Tokyo Metropolitan Central Wholesale Market’s monthly and annual reports. In 2022, the average annual price was ¥4,998 and had remained in that range of around ¥5,000 for the last five years. Since 2009 and 2010, when the price was roughly ¥2,300, it has been rising sharply, reaching the ¥4,000 to ¥5,000 range in 2012 and exceeding ¥5,000 in 2019.

[![Average Eel Prices at Tokyo Metropolitan Central Wholesale Market](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2435273/2435273.png)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2435273/2435273.png)

Eel, known as *unagi*, is a quintessential ingredient and a mainstay of Japanese food culture. However, in the period 2009 through 2012, catches of juvenile glass eels in Japan fell drastically. Whereas previous catches reached 200,000 to 300,000 tons, the volume had dropped to less than 100,000 tons, so in February 2013, the Ministry of the Environment designated the Japanese eel as endangered (Class IB on its red list, meaning the eel is likely to become extinct in the future). In June 2014, the International Union for Conservation of Nature added the Japanese eel to its Red List of Threatened Species.

Since then, progress has been made in conserving resources in Japan, such as by introducing a permit system for eel farmers to limit breeding and reducing the volume of catches made of eels heading to spawning areas.

It is now 10 years since Japanese eels were classified as endangered. The supply of *unagi*, which had fallen to around 32,000 tons in 2013, has been gradually recovering, reaching more than 60,000 tons in 2021.

[![The Unagi Supply in Japan](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2435274/2435274.png)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2435274/2435274.png)

The graph above shows a breakdown of how the supply of eels has been changing in Japan over the last six decades. Currently, only around 60 tons are caught by fisheries. In 2021, 42,000 tons, or two-thirds of the total supply, was imported from countries like China and Taiwan, and 20,000 tons, or one-third, was produced through domestic aquaculture.

From the 1980s onward, Japan imported large quantities of *unagi*, peaking at 133,000 tons in 2000. Many were European eels that had been produced in China, but a drop in resources has meant a decline in Chinese eel farming. The introduction of trade restrictions also means it is no longer possible to increase supply in Japan by boosting imports.

The *unagi* produced using aquaculture are currently all glass eels that have been caught in the wild and then raised in captivity. The ecology of eels is still largely unknown and due to *unagi* being traded at high prices, it is possible that if not properly managed, resources will be depleted.

While research is being carried out in Japan to artificially hatch glass eels and raise them, there is no commercial outlook as yet.

*(Translated from Japanese. Banner photo © Pixta.)*

The prices for other temples range from ¥500 to ¥1,000. Please note though that in the *kōyō* (autumn foliage) season and special viewing periods, some places charge a separate fee.

In April 2023, Kinkakuji and Ryōanji, renowned for its rock garden, both decided to raise their admission fees by ¥100.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ed/Reciprocal_Access_Agreements_of_Japan_%282026%29.png/250px-Reciprocal_Access_Agreements_of_Japan_%282026%29.png)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Reciprocal_Access_Agreements_of_Japan_(2026).png)

Reciprocal access agreements of Japan

A **reciprocal access agreement** (**RAA**) ([Japanese](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_language "Japanese language"): 部隊間協力円滑化協定, [lit.](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literal_translation "Literal translation") 'force-to-force cooperation facilitation agreement')[[1]](#cite_note-MOFAJ20230111-1) refers to a bilateral defense and security pacts between governments that provides shared military training and military operations.[[2]](#cite_note-:0-2)[[3]](#cite_note-:1-3)[[4]](#cite_note-:2-4)[[5]](#cite_note-:4-5) It is an agreement built to create a framework for the two cooperating countries to move their military force whenever required, and also provides a pathway for goods to be imported and exported from one country to the other through following the movement of visiting military forces.[[2]](#cite_note-:0-2)

RAAs have been established between [Japan](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan") and [Australia](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia"), Japan and the [United Kingdom](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") and Japan and the [Philippines](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippines "Philippines").[[6]](#cite_note-:12-6)[[7]](#cite_note-7) For Australia, the signing of a reciprocal access agreement has later been used to further strengthen ties with other countries like [India](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India") and the [United States](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"), and to also renew old pacts like the Joint Declaration on Security Cooperation (JDSC).[[8]](#cite_note-8)

The following RAAs have been signed and are currently active.

### Japan and Australia

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Reciprocal_access_agreement&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Japan and Australia")]

Discussions over signing of the **Japan-Australia Reciprocal Access Agreement** ([Japanese](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_language "Japanese language"): 日豪円滑化協定), officially **Agreement between Japan and Australia concerning the facilitation of reciprocal access and cooperation between the Self-Defense Forces of Japan and the Australian Defence Force**[[9]](#cite_note-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10) began in 2014 and was to be the second significant security pact Japan has made with another country ever since the [1960 Status of Forces Agreement](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S.–Japan_Status_of_Forces_Agreement "U.S.–Japan Status of Forces Agreement") with the United States.[[3]](#cite_note-:1-3) It was signed during a virtual summit on 6 January 2022 by Japanese Prime Minister [Fumio Kishida](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fumio_Kishida "Fumio Kishida") and Australian Prime Minister [Scott Morrison](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Morrison "Scott Morrison") after the former declined all overseas travel due to the increasing [COVID-19](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19 "COVID-19") cases at the time.[[5]](#cite_note-:4-5)

The pact has since then risen in prominence against the recent geopolitical tension and increasing competition in the [Indo-Pacific](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indo-Pacific "Indo-Pacific") space. Japan and Australia have shared concerns over [China](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China")'s growing maritime activities in the [South China Sea](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_China_Sea "South China Sea"), along with the concerns over a potential conflict with the [Chinese Communist Party](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party").[[4]](#cite_note-:2-4)[[11]](#cite_note-11) This was later exacerbated by China's imposement of economic and diplomatic sanctions in response to Australia's call for promoting and inquiry into the origins of the COVID-19 virus.[[12]](#cite_note-12)

On 22 October 2022, Prime Ministers [Anthony Albanese](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Albanese "Anthony Albanese") of Australia and Kishida Fumio further used the RAA to revise an old pact known as the Joint Declaration on Security Cooperation (JDSC).[[13]](#cite_note-13)[[14]](#cite_note-14) The initial JDSC was signed back in 2007 and signed by Prime Ministers [John Howard](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Howard "John Howard") and [Abe Shinzo](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shinzo_Abe "Shinzo Abe"), in part as a response to the growing security ties in the wake of the [September 11 attacks](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11_attacks "September 11 attacks"). It was initially a non-binding security agreement, but the revision has made it a binding treaty between the two countries, and has allowed a more efficient utilization of the RAA.[[15]](#cite_note-15)

The Japan Australia RAA has also been used as a stepping stone to strengthen the ties between India and the United States,

which formed an official grouping with Japan and Australia known as the [Quadrilateral Security Dialogue](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadrilateral_Security_Dialogue "Quadrilateral Security Dialogue"), or simply "The Quad".[[3]](#cite_note-:1-3)[[4]](#cite_note-:2-4)[[16]](#cite_note-16) This group was initially formed in 2004 after the [2004 Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Indian_Ocean_earthquake_and_tsunami "2004 Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami"). There was initially some discussion over forming joint military exercises between the four nations back in 2007, but that was later scrapped due to heavy criticism from China. This was later rectified in 2020, with the four nations holding their first joint military exercise. This was done in part due to the growing concerns over [Beijing](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing")'s actions in backing [Moscow](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow "Moscow") and their distancing from the West.[[17]](#cite_note-17)

### Japan and the United Kingdom

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Reciprocal_access_agreement&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Japan and the United Kingdom")]

On 5 May 2022, during an in-person meeting in [Downing Street](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downing_Street "Downing Street"), [United Kingdom](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") Prime Minister [Boris Johnson](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_Johnson "Boris Johnson") and Kishida agreed to begin discussions over signing an agreement similar to the RAA between Australia and Japan.[[18]](#cite_note-:3-18)[[19]](#cite_note-19)[[20]](#cite_note-20)[[21]](#cite_note-21) Similar to the original Japan Australia RAA, this was done to both ease the hosting of joint military exercises and to simplify the process of bringing troops from one country to another. In addition, this new agreement has allowed Japan to [jointly develop a next-generation fighter jet](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Combat_Air_Programme "Global Combat Air Programme"). This would be the first time Japan has worked on a major military project with another country other than the United States.[[22]](#cite_note-22)

On the 11 January 2023, Japanese Prime Minister [Fumio Kishida](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fumio_Kishida "Fumio Kishida") and UK Prime Minister [Rishi Sunak](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak "Rishi Sunak") signed the **Japan-UK Reciprocal Access Agreement** ([Japanese](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_language "Japanese language"): 日英部隊間協力円滑化協定), officially **Agreement between Japan and the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland concerning the facilitation of reciprocal access and cooperation between the Self-Defense Forces of Japan and the Armed Forces of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland**[[1]](#cite_note-MOFAJ20230111-1) during Kishida's visit to London[[23]](#cite_note-:02-23)[[6]](#cite_note-:12-6) that will allow both nations to deploy troops in each other's countries. The UK will be the first European country to have such a reciprocal access agreement with Japan, with the UK government describing the pact as the most important of its type since the [1902 Anglo-Japanese Alliance](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Japanese_Alliance "Anglo-Japanese Alliance").[[24]](#cite_note-24)

Signing ceremony for the Philippine RAA on 8 July 2024

On 3 November 2023, Japan and the [Philippines](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippines "Philippines") announced that they had begun talks for a Reciprocal Access Agreement.[[25]](#cite_note-25)[[26]](#cite_note-26) On 6 November 2023, Philippine [Defense Secretary](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_National_Defense_(Philippines) "Secretary of National Defense (Philippines)") [Gilberto Teodoro](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilberto_Teodoro "Gilberto Teodoro") stated that his country wanted to reach an agreement "at the soonest possible time".[[27]](#cite_note-27)

“Scholarships” provided by the Japan Student Services Organization are mainly loans that students are required to pay back.

* English
* 日本語
* 简体字
* 繁體字
* Français
* Español
* العربية
* Русский

The Japan Student Services Organization is responsible for the “scholarship” program funded by the Japanese government. The program budget for fiscal 2023 was ¥1.2 trillion. While grants accounted for ¥260.1 billion (22.6%), interest-free and interest-bearing loan-based scholarships that require repayment stood at ¥890.7 billion, or almost 80% of the total.

[![FY 2023 Scholarship Program](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2470872/2470872.png)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2470872/2470872.png)

In a survey conducted by SMBC Consumer Finance on teenagers’ thinking about money, respondents were asked who was responsible for repaying a scholarship if they used one. The results revealed that 69.1% of university students (including students retaking exams and vocational students) and 61.7% of high school students said “myself,” an indication that students who were depending on their parents financially were in the minority.

Grant-based scholarships were only introduced in 2017, so it could be it is still deeply instilled that a scholarship is something that needs to be paid back.

[![Person responsible for repaying scholarship money](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2470737/2470737.png)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2470737/2470737.png)

It is not, however, easy for students to repay loans themselves. According to JASSO data, the average total loaned amount per scholarship student whose loan ended in March 2022 was ¥2.2 million (interest free) and ¥3.4 million (interest bearing). As of fiscal 2021, there were 128,000 people struggling to repay their loans (defined as being three months or more in arrears). While the figure is dropping, it is an issue that cannot be overlooked.

[![Number of people in arrears by more than 3 monthsPerson responsible for repaying scholarship money](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2474490/2474490.png)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2474490/2474490.png)

The system of grant scholarships with no repayment requirement was launched in fiscal 2017, intended for students from low-income, tax-exempt households. From fiscal 2024, this support will be expanded to include middle-income households with three or more children. The annual income cap for eligibility will be raised from the current ¥3.8 million to around ¥6 million. It is expected that the number of people newly eligible will increase by up to 200,000.

*(Translated from Japanese. Banner photo: © Pixta.)*

A report in Japan found that many older people are hesitant about writing their will.

* English
* 日本語
* 简体字
* 繁體字
* Français
* Español
* العربية
* Русский

The Japanese legal office Authense LPC published its 2023 annual report on wills, based on internet surveys and other data. It found that overall, 65.5% of those aged 50 or older are either “very interested” or “somewhat interested” in drawing up a will. However, the breakdown by age bracket shows that the level of interest declines the older one gets, from 71.3% among those in their fifties to 64.6% and 55.8%, respectively, among those in their sixties and seventies. Perhaps the decrease reflects a tendency to not want to face the reality that a will represents.

[![What is your attitude toward creating a will?](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2519820/2519820.png)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2519820/2519820.png)

Only 8.5% of the respondents said that they definitely planned to make a will, while 25.1% said that they probably would, for a total of 35.6%. The three most common reasons cited for not creating a will were “I have a small estate,” “I’m still healthy,” and “it’s not really relevant to me yet.”

Among younger people, there was a lower level of intention to create a will at some point, with a total of 27.1% of those aged 20 to 49 saying they would either definitely or probably draw up a will.

[![Do you have plans to create a will?](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2503502/2503502.png)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2503502/2503502.png)

[![Do you have plans to create a will?](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2504284/2504284.png)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2504284/2504284.png)

The percentage of those who have already discussed a will with their children is higher among those aged 70 and over, at 18.3%, while 62.5% of that age group are either interested in discussing or intend to discuss the issue with their children. However, about half of those who have already talked about a will with their children do not actually intend to create one. This contradiction speaks to the low level of willingness among Japanese to draw up a will.

[![Do you intend to talk about a will with your children?](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2503510/2503510.png)](/en/ncommon/contents/japan-data/2503510/2503510.png)

**Japan–South Korea relations** are the diplomatic relations between [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan") and [South Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea "South Korea"). As the [Sea of Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_of_Japan "Sea of Japan") and the [Korea Strait](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korea_Strait "Korea Strait") geographically separate the two nations, political interactions date back from the 6th century when the [kingdom of Baekje](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baekje "Baekje") (which encompassed much of present-day South Korea) officially established relations with the [Yamato Kingship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yamato_Kingship "Yamato Kingship") of Japan. During the ancient era, the southern region of the [Korean Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Peninsula "Korean Peninsula") served as the closest port for economic trade and [cultural exchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_influence_on_Japanese_culture "Korean influence on Japanese culture") between the [Japanese archipelago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_archipelago "Japanese archipelago") and mainland Asia. Such relations would continue by the late 19th century when both [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meiji_Restoration "Meiji Restoration") and [Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Empire "Korean Empire") underwent [modernisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernisation "Modernisation") from Western powers up until 1910, when [Korea became a colony of Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korea_under_Japanese_rule "Korea under Japanese rule").

Shortly after gaining independence from the Japanese surrender at the end of [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") in 1945, [Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korea "Korea") was [divided](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Division_of_Korea "Division of Korea") into two states. During the [Korean War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_War "Korean War"), Japan took part in aiding South Korea by providing military supplies to US and UN forces against the communist-led [North Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Korea "North Korea"). Japan and South Korea formally established diplomatic relations in December 1965, under the [Treaty on Basic Relations Between Japan and the Republic of Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_on_Basic_Relations_Between_Japan_and_the_Republic_of_Korea "Treaty on Basic Relations Between Japan and the Republic of Korea"), with Japan recognising South Korea as the only legitimate government in the Korean Peninsula. Japan and South Korea share many cultural, economic, and military ties. ## 6. Strongest contrary evidence and unresolved gaps

- **Chapter 7B counter:** The LDP slush-fund scandal is the strongest contrary evidence; it is documented, ongoing, and implicates the entire LDP apparatus including factions adjacent to Kishida (though not Kishida personally). The removal of four cabinet ministers on 14 December 2023 and Kishida's eventual January 2024 dissolution of Kōchikai and 14 August 2024 resignation are the strongest 7B-specific actions by Kishida in 2023.
- **Chapter 4B counter:** The LGBT Understanding Promotion Act, while a first, was criticized for weak language ("unfair discrimination") and no penalties; the penal code still required spousal authorization for abortion; the ICRRA amendment permits deportation of repeat asylum applicants.
- **Chapter 2B counter:** The Myanmar incidents (Yokogawa Bridge Corp.; misuse of Japan-funded ships by Myanmar military) show that Japan-funded entities were diverted to military use; Kishida's response was limited to Tokyo confirming the misuse.
- **Chapter 3B counter:** The ICRRA amendment and the foreign technical intern program reforms that have not progressed are the strongest adverse evidence for vulnerable-group protection.

  - No public-asset-disclosure document for Kishida 2023; personal-asset narrative relies on the Unification Church link (associates, not personal).
